title: Method of Moments, Minimum Chi-square and Least Squares
breadcrumb: Statistical Inference → Point Estimation → Estimators you can write down without a likelihood
engineName: Estimation and inference — matching what you observe to what the model predicts
provenance: Review pass, October 2026: 5 per-scene quick checks added on theory, worked and explore scenes from a third-party module review, each read for correctness before import; a further set offered for completion and guided scenes was declined, since those scenes already end with the learner writing an answer. Theory, worked examples and practice authored for this platform against the UGC NET Statistics syllabus. Previous-year questions are stored separately and carry their exam cycle.
objectives: Set up and solve the moment equations for a one- or two-parameter family, choosing raw or central moments to keep the algebra short.
State what the method of moments guarantees (consistency, asymptotic normality) and what it does not (unbiasedness, efficiency, a legal estimate).
Recognise the two families the exam uses against the method: U(a,b), where the estimate can be impossible, and Cauchy, where there is no moment to match.
Define the minimum chi-square and modified minimum chi-square estimators, and say what data they need.
Derive the least squares normal equations as moment conditions, and see least squares as one more instance of the same idea.

prereq.name: Population and sample moments
prereq.why: The whole method is one line: set m_r' equal to μ_r' and solve. If the notation is not automatic, fix that first.

prereq.name: Mean and variance of standard families
prereq.why: You need E[X] and Var(X) for the gamma, uniform, exponential and normal from memory — the moment equations start there.

prereq.name: Maximum likelihood estimation
prereq.why: Every comparison in this topic is against the MLE: sometimes the two coincide, usually the MLE is more efficient, occasionally the moment estimator is the only one you can write down.

refs.title: Method of Moments
refs.why: The cleanest statement of both forms of the method, with the Bernoulli, normal and gamma worked out (Examples 1-7 to 1-10). Example 1-10 redoes the normal by the second form and shows it is less work — the same labour-saving point scene 3 makes. CC BY-NC, no login.

refs.title: Parametric models and method of moments
refs.why: Six worked examples (Poisson, exponential, normal, gamma) and then bias, variance and MSE computed for the moment estimators themselves — which is what scene 9 asks you to do. It does not cover consistency or asymptotic normality, so take those from scene 3 here.

refs.title: Paths to least squares
refs.why: Arrives at least squares four separate ways — risk minimisation, maximum likelihood with normal errors, a Bayesian posterior mean, and a moment condition. Read it after scene 11, which derives the last of those. It is the best short argument that these 'different methods' are one idea seen from different sides.

sheet: Method of moments: equate the first k sample moments to the first k population moments and solve for the k parameters.
Raw moments: m_r' = (1/n)Σxᵢ^r  matched to  μ_r' = E[X^r].  Central: m₂ = (1/n)Σ(xᵢ−x̄)² matched to Var(X). Use whichever makes the algebra shorter.
One unknown → one equation (usually E[X] = x̄). Two unknowns → add Var(X) = m₂.
Gamma(α, β) with mean αβ, variance αβ²:   β̃ = m₂/x̄,   α̃ = x̄²/m₂.
N(μ,σ²):   μ̃ = x̄,   σ̃² = m₂ = (1/n)Σ(xᵢ−x̄)².  Note the divisor n, not n−1 — the moment estimator of σ² is biased.
Exponential(rate λ):   λ̃ = 1/x̄ = n/ΣX.  Same as the MLE, and biased: E[λ̃] = nλ/(n−1), bias = λ/(n−1).
GUARANTEED: consistency (WLLN plus continuous mapping) and asymptotic normality.
NOT guaranteed: unbiasedness, efficiency, uniqueness, or even an estimate inside the parameter space.
Fails outright when the moment does not exist — Cauchy has no mean, so there is nothing to match.
Minimum chi-square: choose θ to minimise Σ (Oᵢ − npᵢ(θ))² / (npᵢ(θ)) over the k cells. Needs grouped or categorical data.

Modified minimum chi-square puts Oᵢ in the denominator instead: Σ (Oᵢ − npᵢ(θ))² / Oᵢ. It is easier to minimise, but requires Oᵢ > 0 in every included cell; a zero observed count makes the denominator undefined.
For multinomial data, minimum chi-square, modified minimum chi-square and ML are all BAN and asymptotically equivalent.
Least squares: minimise Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)². Needs no distributional assumption; coincides with ML when the errors are normal.
The normal equations ARE moment conditions: E[ε] = 0 and E[Xε] = 0 in their sample form.
cards: State the method of moments in one sentence.
Equate the first k sample moments to the corresponding population moments and solve the resulting k equations for the k unknown parameters.
What does the method of moments guarantee?
Consistency and asymptotic normality. Not unbiasedness, not efficiency, not a legal estimate.
Moment estimators for Gamma(α, β)?
β̃ = m₂/x̄ and α̃ = x̄²/m₂, from αβ = x̄ and αβ² = m₂.
Moment estimator of θ for U(0,θ), and its defect?
θ̃ = 2x̄. It can come out smaller than the largest observation, which is impossible — the MLE x₍ₙ₎ never does.
Why does the method fail for the Cauchy distribution?
The Cauchy has no finite mean, so there is no first population moment to equate the sample mean to.
Moment estimator of σ² in N(μ,σ²), and is it unbiased?
σ̃² = (1/n)Σ(xᵢ−x̄)². Biased: E[σ̃²] = (n−1)σ²/n. Multiplying by n/(n−1) gives the unbiased s².
Write the minimum chi-square criterion.
Minimise Σ (Oᵢ − npᵢ(θ))²/(npᵢ(θ)) over θ, summed over the cells. The modified version divides by Oᵢ instead.
In what sense are the normal equations moment conditions?
They are the sample versions of E[ε] = 0 and E[Xε] = 0 — the residuals are made to have zero mean and zero correlation with the regressor.
When do least squares and maximum likelihood agree?
When the errors are independent normal with constant variance: maximising that likelihood is minimising the sum of squares.
Why is the method of moments still worth knowing if the MLE is better?
It is almost always computable in closed form, it needs no likelihood, and it supplies the starting value for the iteration that finds the MLE.
traps: Using n−1 in the moment estimator of σ². The method gives the divisor n; the n−1 version is a separate, bias-corrected estimator.
Quoting the moment estimate for U(0,θ) without checking it against the largest observation.
Claiming the method of moments is unbiased because it is consistent. The two are different properties.
Matching E[X²] when Var(X) would have given a one-line solution, or the reverse — pick the form that cancels.
Treating minimum chi-square as a general method. It needs the data grouped into cells with expected frequencies.

tricks.why: Count the parameters first. Starting with one equation for a two-parameter family is the commonest way to waste time.
Var ÷ mean cancels the shape in the gamma and leaves the scale alone. Look for it whenever a parameter multiplies both.
The moment estimator of σ² is Σ(xᵢ−x̄)²/n. The n−1 version is a separate, bias-corrected estimator.
The Cauchy has no finite first moment, so there is nothing to equate x̄ to. The method fails, and that failure IS the answer.

shortcuts: Gamma(α,β): β̃ = m₂/x̄ and α̃ = x̄²/m₂.
When the first moment carries no parameter — as for U(−θ,θ) — skip it and match the variance.
Least squares is the method of moments applied to E[ε] = 0 and E[Xε] = 0.
remember: Guaranteed: consistency and asymptotic normality. NOT guaranteed: unbiasedness, efficiency, uniqueness, or a legal estimate.
Always check the answer against the parameter space — and against the sample maximum for a uniform.

traps: The divisor in σ̃² is n, not n−1.
θ̃ = 2x̄ for U(0,θ) can be less than x₍ₙ₎, and then it is not an estimate at all.
No moments, no method — the Cauchy has no mean.
Least squares needs no normality; it only coincides with ML when the errors are normal.

scenes.title: Before the lesson — four things it will assume
scenes.objective: Get the moments of the standard families and the moment/variance identity back to automatic, since every equation in this topic starts there.
body: The method of moments is the easiest estimation method to state and the easiest to fumble. Stating it takes one line: set the sample moments equal to the population moments and solve. Fumbling it takes one forgotten formula — the variance of a uniform, say, or the rate-versus-scale convention for the gamma.
So this check is mostly recall of standard results. That is deliberate: in the exam these are not derived, they are remembered, and a two year gap is exactly long enough to lose them.

items.ask: Define the r-th population moment and the r-th sample moment, and state what the method of moments does with them.
items.recall: μ_r′ = E[Xʳ] and m_r′ = (1/n)Σxᵢʳ. For k unknown parameters, set m_r′ = μ_r′(θ) for r = 1,…,k and solve the k equations.
refresh: The population moment is a property of the model and so is a function of θ: for an exponential with rate λ, μ₁′ = 1/λ. The sample moment is a number computed from the data and knows nothing about θ.

The method just equates them and solves. One unknown, one equation: 1/λ = x̄ gives λ̃ = 1/x̄. Two unknowns, two equations — which is where the second moment comes in and where the arithmetic starts to bite.

A word on notation, since exam papers use both. The prime marks a raw moment, about zero. Moments about the mean are written without it: μ₂ = Var(X). Mixing the two is the commonest source of a wrong sign in this topic.

items.ask: From memory: E[X] and Var(X) for the exponential, U(a,b), gamma and normal.
items.recall: Exponential with rate λ: 1/λ and 1/λ². U(a,b): (a+b)/2 and (b−a)²/12. Gamma with shape α and rate β: α/β and α/β². Normal(μ,σ²): μ and σ².
refresh: Carry these four as a block, because the moment equations begin with them and there is no time to derive them in the exam.
Exponential(λ): mean 1/λ, variance 1/λ². The exponential is a gamma with shape 1, which is the quickest way to recover it if you blank.
U(a,b): mean is the midpoint (a+b)/2; variance is (b−a)²/12. The 12 is the one number people lose. Sanity check: U(0,1) has variance 1/12 ≈ 0.083, which is right for a spread of one unit.

Gamma: with shape α and rate β, mean α/β and variance α/β². If the book uses scale θ = 1/β instead, the mean is αθ and the variance αθ². Read which convention a question is using before you write anything — the two differ by a reciprocal and the options will include both answers.

items.ask: How do E[X²], Var(X) and E[X] relate, and why does the second moment equation nearly always use that identity?
items.recall: E[X²] = Var(X) + (E[X])². The second sample moment (1/n)Σxᵢ² estimates E[X²], not the variance — so you convert the model's variance into a second moment before equating.
refresh: Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])² rearranged. Nothing more, but it is used in every two-parameter moment problem.
See why. For N(μ,σ²), the two moment equations are μ = x̄ and E[X²] = σ² + μ² = (1/n)Σxᵢ². Substituting the first into the second gives σ̃² = (1/n)Σxᵢ² − x̄² = (1/n)Σ(xᵢ−x̄)².

Note what came out: the divisor is n, not n−1. The method of moments estimator of a variance is the biased one, and the lesson returns to that — the method makes no promise of unbiasedness, only of consistency.

items.ask: What does least squares minimise, and what are the normal equations for fitting a straight line?
items.recall: It minimises Σ(yᵢ − a − bxᵢ)². Setting the two partial derivatives to zero gives b̂ = Σ(xᵢ−x̄)(yᵢ−ȳ)/Σ(xᵢ−x̄)² and â = ȳ − b̂x̄.
refresh: You differentiate the sum of squared vertical deviations with respect to a and then b, set both to zero, and solve. The two resulting equations are called the normal equations.

Both formulas carry a reading worth keeping. b̂ is a ratio of the sample covariance of x and y to the variance of x. And â = ȳ − b̂x̄ says the fitted line passes through (x̄, ȳ) whatever the slope — a free check on any numerical answer.
The lesson compares all three methods on the same footing, so you need this one in the same form as the other two: an estimating criterion, differentiated, set to zero.

scenes.title: Match what you see to what the model predicts
scenes.objective: Get the one idea behind the whole topic before any algebra.
body: Your model says the mean of X is some expression in θ. Your data have a mean you can compute. The method of moments does the obvious thing: it sets the two equal and solves for θ.
If there are two unknowns, one equation is not enough, so you add the next moment — usually the variance — and solve the pair. k unknowns, k moments, k equations. That is the entire method.

Why bother, when maximum likelihood is better behaved? Three reasons, and the exam uses all three. The moment estimator can almost always be written down in closed form, where the likelihood equation may need a computer. It needs no distributional assumption beyond the moments themselves. And when an iterative routine does go looking for the MLE, the moment estimate is what it starts from.

What you give up is sharpness. The method looks only at the first few moments and throws the rest of the sample's information away, so it is usually less efficient than the MLE. It is generally biased. And in two notorious cases it either produces an impossible answer or cannot be started at all — both of which you will meet in this lesson, because both are examined.

Keep the method's status clear in your head: it is a reliable way to GET an estimator, not a claim that the estimator is good. Those are separate questions, answered by the tools from the last three topics.

aside.body: The weak law of large numbers says the sample moments converge in probability to the population moments. If the parameter is a continuous function of those moments, the estimator inherits the convergence. That is the whole proof of consistency, and it is also the reason nothing stronger is promised.

ask.label: Ask Claude where this method sits among the others
ask.prompt: A UGC NET Statistics (JRF) candidate is studying the method of moments after covering sufficiency, Rao–Blackwell, MLE and the Cramér–Rao bound. In under 160 words, plain text, place the method of moments against those: what question it answers that they do not, and why a method with weaker properties is still on the syllabus. Do not list the steps of the method.

scenario.teaser: Every flood defence in the country is sized by a method-of-moments fit.
scenario.title: Sizing a spillway from 40 years of annual peak flows
body: A dam spillway has to pass the 100-year flood. The hydrologist has one number per year — the annual peak discharge — and perhaps forty of them. From that, a design flow with an exceedance probability of 0.01 must be produced, and defended at a public inquiry.

The standard practice is to fit a two-parameter distribution to the annual maxima, commonly a gamma or a Gumbel, and read the quantile off the fitted curve. The fitting is done by the method of moments: set the mean of the distribution equal to the sample mean, the variance equal to the sample variance, and solve.

Why not maximum likelihood, which is more efficient? Three reasons, all of them the ones this lesson gives. The moment estimates are closed-form, so they can be computed and audited on a spreadsheet by a reviewer who is not a statistician. They require no iteration that might fail to converge on a short record. And national design guidance has to be reproducible — two engineers with the same data must get the same answer, which an iterative optimiser does not guarantee.

The cost is efficiency. With forty observations the moment estimate of the shape parameter is noticeably noisier than the MLE, and the 100-year quantile inherits that noise. Practitioners handle this by reporting confidence bands around the design flow rather than pretending the point estimate is exact.

There is also a trap this lesson has already shown you. If the sample variance is large relative to the squared mean, the gamma shape estimate α̃ = x̄²/m₂ comes out below 1 — a legal value, but one implying an infinite density at zero flow. If it comes out negative, which a short skewed record can produce for other distributions, the estimate is outside the parameter space and must be reported as such rather than quietly truncated.
scenario.q: A record gives x̄ = 400 m³/s and m₂ = 160,000. What are the gamma moment estimates, and what do they say?
scenario.answer: β̃ = m₂/x̄ = 160000/400 = 400 and α̃ = x̄²/m₂ = 160000/160000 = 1. A shape of exactly 1 is the exponential distribution, so the record is consistent with exponentially distributed annual peaks of mean 400 — which is the classic signature of a variance equal to the squared mean. That is a meaningful finding rather than a failure: it tells the hydrologist the data carry no evidence of the extra shape flexibility the gamma offers, and that the simpler one-parameter model would do.
scenario.link: The same moment fit is used for wind-speed distributions in turbine siting and for particle-size distributions in process engineering — anywhere a closed-form, auditable fit matters more than the last few percent of efficiency.

scenes.title: Where the moment estimator lands
scenes.objective: See a case where the moment estimator and the MLE are the same point.
body: Exponential with rate λ, so E[X] = 1/λ. The moment equation is 1/λ = x̄, giving λ̃ = 1/x̄ = n/Σxᵢ.

The readout labelled λ̂ = n/Σxᵢ is exactly that number. With n = 4 and Σxᵢ = 16 it is 0.25, and the curve peaks there. For this family the moment estimator and the maximum likelihood estimator are the same estimator, arrived at by two completely different arguments — one matching a mean, one maximising a product.

Drag the candidate λ slider away from the peak and watch the likelihood ratio fall. That is the likelihood's opinion of values the moment equation would never have proposed. Now change n and Σxᵢ: the two estimators move together, always, because 1/x̄ IS the maximiser here.

Do not generalise from this. The coincidence happens when the parameter appears in the mean in a simple enough way — the exponential, the Poisson, the Bernoulli, the normal mean. For the uniform, the gamma shape, and most two-parameter problems, the two estimators are different numbers, and the MLE is the better one.
One thing the coincidence does NOT buy: unbiasedness. λ̃ = n/ΣX is the MLE and the moment estimator, and it is biased upward. Scene 9 computes by how much.

ask.q: Why does matching the first population moment to the first sample moment produce a method-of-moments estimator?
ask.nudge: The sample moment is used as an estimate of the corresponding population moment, yielding an equation in the unknown parameter.

scenes.title: The method, both forms, and what it promises
scenes.objective: Set the equations up correctly and know exactly which properties you may claim.

blocks.body: For a family with k unknown parameters θ₁,…,θ_k, equate the first k population moments to the first k sample moments and solve. The solution θ̃ is the method of moments estimator (MME).
μ_r'(θ) = E[X^r]  set equal to  m_r' = (1/n) Σ xᵢ^r ,   for r = 1, …, k.
E[X] = x̄   and   Var(X) = m₂ = (1/n) Σ (xᵢ − x̄)² ,   then higher central moments if k > 2.

Whichever cancels. Form 2 is almost always shorter for a two-parameter family, because the variance is usually a cleaner expression in θ than E[X²] is. Penn State's Example 1-10 redoes the normal by Form 2 after Example 1-8 did it by Form 1, and the saving is obvious. The two forms give the same estimator — they are algebraically equivalent, since m₂ = m₂' − (m₁')².

blocks.h: The procedure, in the order that avoids dead ends
blocks.body:
1. Count the unknown parameters: that is how many equations you need.
2. Write E[X], and Var(X) if there are two, as expressions in the parameters.
3. Set them equal to x̄ and m₂.
4. Solve — divide one equation by the other first if a parameter appears in both.
5. CHECK the answer lies in the parameter space.

Under identification and continuity of the inverse moment map, convergence of the sample moments gives consistency. Asymptotic normality additionally requires a central limit theorem for the sample moments and a nonsingular Jacobian of the moment map. These are regularity conditions, not unconditional guarantees.

Unbiasedness — σ̃² for the normal is biased, and λ̃ for the exponential rate is biased. Efficiency — the method uses only k moments, not the whole likelihood, so its asymptotic variance is generally larger than the MLE's. Uniqueness — a different choice of moments can give a different estimator. And admissibility of the answer: the estimate can land outside the parameter space, which scene 8 shows.

blocks.h: When the method cannot be started
blocks.body: The moments you want to match have to exist. The Cauchy distribution has no finite mean, so there is no first population moment and the method is simply unavailable — the sample mean of a Cauchy sample does not settle down as n grows. This is a standing exam question, and the correct answer is that the method fails, not that you should use a median.

blocks.h: Sufficiency, and why the method ignores it
blocks.body: x̄ and m₂ are not in general sufficient, so the moment estimator can discard information that the likelihood keeps. That is the structural reason for the efficiency loss, and it links this topic straight back to sufficiency: the MLE is a function of the sufficient statistic, and the MME need not be.

flow.title: The method of moments, with the check that most answers omit
flow.alt: Decision chart for method of moments estimation

nodes.label: Do the first k population moments exist?
No moments, no method — e.g. the Cauchy
Write E[X], and Var(X) if k = 2, in the parameters
Set equal to x̄ and m₂; divide one by the other to eliminate
Does the solution lie INSIDE the parameter space?
Inadmissible — say so and give the MLE instead

flow.note: The last diamond is the one that is skipped. For U(0,θ) the estimate 2x̄ can land below the largest observation, where the likelihood is exactly zero — and that is the examinable point, not a mistake to hide.

ask.q: When the number of unknown parameters exceeds the number of moment equations, what must you do before claiming a unique method-of-moments estimate?
ask.nudge: Choose additional moments or another identification strategy; the original equations may not determine a unique solution.

scenes.title: Worked in full — the gamma, where one equation is not enough
scenes.objective: Run a genuine two-parameter moment calculation end to end.
scenes.problem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Gamma with shape α and scale β, so E[X] = αβ and Var(X) = αβ². A sample gives x̄ = 6 and m₂ = 4. Find the method of moments estimators of α and β, and evaluate them.

steps.say: Count the unknowns, so you know how many equations to write.
steps.math: Two parameters, α and β  ⇒  two moment equations.
steps.why: This is step one for a reason. Writing one equation and then discovering you cannot solve it wastes the time the second equation would have cost.

steps.say: Write the two equations, using the mean and the variance rather than E[X] and E[X²].
steps.why: Var(X) = αβ² is a cleaner expression in α and β than E[X²] = αβ²(α+1) would be. This is Form 2 earning its keep.

steps.say: Divide (ii) by (i). The shape cancels and β falls out alone.
steps.why: Dividing is the move to look for whenever the same parameter multiplies both sides. It turns a simultaneous system into two one-line solutions.

steps.say: Substitute back into (i) for the shape.
steps.math: α = x̄ / β = x̄ / (m₂/x̄) = x̄² / m₂
steps.why: Note the shape estimator is a ratio of the squared mean to the variance — large relative to its spread means a large shape parameter, which is the right direction.
Keep the fraction until the end. Rounding β to 0.67 and then computing α from it introduces error for no reason.
Thirty seconds, and it catches an inverted ratio or a dropped square. Always do it: the moment equations are the one place where the check is this easy.

scenes.after: The pattern generalises to every two-parameter problem on this syllabus: write the mean and the variance, divide to eliminate one parameter, substitute back, check. If the division does not simplify, you have probably chosen the harder of the two forms — try the other.

ask.q: In the Gamma example, why are two equations needed and how do you check the resulting parameter estimates?
ask.nudge: There are two unknown parameters; solve the two moment equations and check both estimates lie in the parameter space.

scenes.title: Pause and recall
scenes.objective: Retrieve before reading on — this is where the retention comes from.
scenes.intro: Answer each in your head before revealing. Correcting a wrong retrieval beats re-reading a right answer.

items.q: State the method of moments in one sentence.
items.a: Equate the first k sample moments to the first k population moments and solve for the k parameters.

items.q: Which two properties does the method guarantee, and which two does it not?
items.a: Guaranteed: consistency and asymptotic normality. Not guaranteed: unbiasedness and efficiency.

items.q: Why is the moment estimator usually less efficient than the MLE?
items.a: It uses only the first k moments, which are not in general sufficient, so it discards information the likelihood keeps.

items.q: Name a family where the method cannot be started at all, and why.
items.a: The Cauchy — it has no finite mean, so there is no first moment to match.

scenes.title: Your turn, with the scaffolding removed — U(a,b)
scenes.objective: Run a two-parameter moment calculation yourself, on the family the exam uses most.
scenes.problem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Uniform on (a, b), with E[X] = (a+b)/2 and Var(X) = (b−a)²/12. A sample gives x̄ = 10 and m₂ = 3. Find the method of moments estimators of a and b, and evaluate them.

steps.why: Two unknowns, two equations. Notice the convenient structure: (i) involves the sum and (ii) the difference, so neither has to be substituted into the other.

steps.say: Solve (ii) for the difference b − a. Take the positive root, since b > a.

blank.prompt: Write b − a in terms of m₂.
blank.hint: Multiply both sides by 12 to get (b−a)² = 12m₂, then take the square root. √12 = 2√3, so the answer can be written either as √(12m₂) or 2√(3m₂).

steps.why: Both forms are the same number. 2√(3m₂) is the one worth memorising, because the 3 under the root is what you will recognise in a multiple-choice option.

steps.say: Combine the sum and the difference. Half the difference, taken either side of the mean, gives the two endpoints.

blank.prompt: Write ã, the estimator of the lower endpoint.
blank.hint: From (i), a + b = 2x̄. You now also have b − a. Subtract the second from the first and halve: a = x̄ − (b−a)/2, and (b−a)/2 = √(3m₂).

steps.why: And by the same step b̃ = x̄ + √(3m₂). The estimates sit symmetrically about the sample mean, which is exactly what a symmetric distribution should give you.

steps.say: Evaluate both at x̄ = 10 and m₂ = 3.

blank.prompt: Give the two numerical estimates, lower then upper.

steps.why: The numbers were chosen to come out whole. In the exam they usually do, and a messy answer is a signal to re-check the 12.
Both reconstructed, so the algebra is sound. What the check cannot tell you is whether the estimate is legal — that needs the sample itself, and it is the subject of the next-but-one scene.

scenes.after: Two special cases fall straight out of this. For U(0,θ), the lower endpoint is known to be 0, so one equation suffices: θ/2 = x̄ gives θ̃ = 2x̄. For U(−θ,θ) the mean is 0 whatever θ is, so the first moment is useless and you must match the variance instead: θ²/3 = m₂, giving θ̃ = √(3m₂). Read the question for which endpoints are known before counting your equations.

scenes.title: The other two methods — minimum chi-square and least squares
scenes.objective: Define both, know what data each needs, and see why they belong in the same lesson.

blocks.body: The data are grouped into k cells with observed frequencies O₁,…,O_k summing to n. The model gives cell probabilities p₁(θ),…,p_k(θ). Choose θ to make the fitted frequencies as close as possible to the observed ones, measured by the Pearson statistic.
minimise over θ:    χ²(θ)  =  Σᵢ ( Oᵢ − n pᵢ(θ) )² / ( n pᵢ(θ) )

minimise over θ:    Σᵢ ( Oᵢ − n pᵢ(θ) )² / Oᵢ
The observed frequency replaces the expected one in the denominator, so θ appears only in the numerator and the minimisation is much easier. This form requires Oᵢ > 0 in every included cell; a zero observed count makes this denominator undefined and needs a different treatment.

For regular identifiable multinomial models with positive cell probabilities and adequate expected counts, the minimum chi-square estimator, the modified minimum chi-square estimator and the MLE are BAN — best asymptotically normal — and asymptotically equivalent. They differ at finite n, and the modified version is the one you can actually solve by hand. Both need the data grouped, with expected cell frequencies not too small, which is the same condition the chi-square goodness-of-fit test carries.

Observations y₁,…,yₙ have means that depend on known constants and unknown parameters: E[yᵢ] = f(xᵢ, β). Choose β to minimise Σ(yᵢ − f(xᵢ, β))². No distribution is assumed — only the form of the mean.

blocks.h: Simple linear regression, the standard result
blocks.body:
minimise Σ(yᵢ − β₀ − β₁xᵢ)²   ⇒   β̂₁ = S_xy / S_xx ,   β̂₀ = ȳ − β̂₁ x̄
where S_xy = Σ(xᵢ−x̄)(yᵢ−ȳ) and S_xx = Σ(xᵢ−x̄)².

If the errors are independent N(0, σ²), maximising the likelihood IS minimising the sum of squares — the two methods give the same β̂. Without normality, OLS is still BLUE under the Gauss–Markov conditions: a correctly specified linear mean, full-column-rank design, zero-mean errors, and uncorrelated errors with a common finite variance. Normality is not required for BLUE; it is what makes least squares coincide with maximum likelihood.

blocks.h: Why these three are one lesson
blocks.body: All three choose θ by making a feature of the model agree with the same feature of the data: moments with moments, fitted frequencies with observed frequencies, fitted values with observed values. None of them maximises a likelihood, and all of them can be computed when the likelihood is intractable. Scene 11 makes the connection exact by deriving least squares as a moment condition.

ask.q: What is being minimised in minimum chi-square and least squares, and how does that differ from matching moments directly?
ask.nudge: Minimum chi-square weights discrepancies between observed and expected cell proportions; least squares minimises a sum of squared residuals.

scenes.title: When the moment estimate is impossible
scenes.objective: See the method produce an answer that the data have already ruled out.
body: U(0,θ). The moment equation is θ/2 = x̄, so θ̃ = 2x̄. Now take this sample of five: 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 4.2.
Σxᵢ = 5.9, so x̄ = 1.18 and θ̃ = 2.36. But one of the observations is 4.2. The method of moments has just told you the upper limit of the distribution is 2.36, having been shown a value of 4.2.

The picture explains why that is not a near miss but a flat impossibility. The likelihood is zero for every θ below the largest observation — no value of θ smaller than 4.2 could have produced a 4.2 — and then falls away as θ⁻ⁿ above it. Drag the θ slider below 4.2 and the likelihood is identically zero. θ̃ = 2.36 sits in that dead region.

The MLE has no such problem: it is θ̂ = x₍ₙ₎ = 4.2, the cliff edge, the smallest θ consistent with the data. Raise the largest observation on the slider and the MLE tracks it exactly, by construction.

What went wrong is that the moment equation looked only at the mean. One large observation lifts the mean a little and the maximum a lot, and for this family it is the maximum that carries the information — x₍ₙ₎ is sufficient for θ, and x̄ is not. The fix, when a question asks for a usable estimator, is to say so: report θ̂ = x₍ₙ₎, or the unbiased (n+1)x₍ₙ₎/n, and state that the moment estimator is inadmissible here because it can fall below the sample maximum.

scenario.teaser: Why an actuary fits claim sizes by moments first and by likelihood second.
scenario.title: The starting value problem, and who solves it
body: An actuary models claim sizes on a motor portfolio as gamma with unknown shape and rate. The likelihood for the gamma shape has no closed-form maximum — it involves the digamma function — so the fit is numerical, and a numerical maximiser has to start somewhere.

The method of moments gives the starting point in one line. Set the first two sample moments equal to their population values and solve: the shape comes out as x̄² divided by the sample variance, and the rate as x̄ divided by the sample variance. No iteration, no derivative, no software beyond a calculator.

Those values are usually close enough that the likelihood maximiser converges in a few steps, and far enough from the boundary that it does not wander off into a region where the shape goes negative. Starting a gamma fit from an arbitrary value is how you get a maximiser that fails to converge, or converges to something a long way from the data.

The division of labour is the point. Moment estimates are consistent, instantaneous and usually less efficient than the MLE; the MLE is efficient but needs a sensible place to begin. The textbook treats them as rival methods; practice treats them as the first and second step of one procedure.
scenario.close: Consistency gets you into the right neighbourhood; the likelihood finds the right house once you are there.

ask.q: What should you do if a method-of-moments solution falls outside the parameter space?
ask.nudge: Recognise that the algebraic solution is not an admissible estimate; do not silently treat it as valid.

scenes.title: Now without the steps — the bias of a moment estimator
scenes.objective: Compute a moment estimator's bias from scratch, and see that consistency did not save it.
scenes.problem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Exponential with rate λ, so E[X] = 1/λ. Find the method of moments estimator of λ. Then, given that ΣXᵢ follows a Gamma(n, rate λ) distribution with E[1/ΣXᵢ] = λ/(n−1) for n > 1, find E[λ̃] and the bias. Evaluate both at n = 5, λ = 2, and say how to remove the bias.
hints: Direction — the moment equation is one line: set E[X] = x̄ and solve for λ. Write the answer in terms of ΣXᵢ rather than x̄ before you take any expectation, because the fact you have been given is about ΣXᵢ.

Method — λ̃ is a constant times 1/ΣXᵢ. Pull the constant out of the expectation and substitute the given value. Do not be tempted to write E[1/X̄] as 1/E[X̄]; that step is false and it is the whole reason this estimator is biased.

Next step — bias is E[λ̃] − λ. Simplify it to a single fraction. Once you see the form of E[λ̃], the multiplier that removes the bias should be obvious, and it will give you an estimator you have already met two topics ago.

solution.say: Set up and solve the moment equation.
Note this is also the MLE for this family, as scene 2 showed. Take its expectation using the given fact.
Subtract λ to get the bias.

solution.math: E[λ̃] = 5(2)/4 = 2.5 ,   bias = 2/4 = 0.5 ,   i.e. 25% too high on average

solution.say: Remove the bias by rescaling. Multiply by (n−1)/n.
Confirm the bias vanishes as n grows, which is consistency at work.
solution.math: λ/(n−1) → 0 as n → ∞,  so λ̃ is consistent despite being biased at every finite n

scenes.answer: λ̃ = 1/x̄ = n/ΣXᵢ. E[λ̃] = nλ/(n−1), so the bias is λ/(n−1) — positive, so the estimator overstates the rate. At n = 5, λ = 2 it averages 2.5, a bias of 0.5. Multiplying by (n−1)/n gives the unbiased (n−1)/ΣXᵢ, which is the UMVUE from the Lehmann–Scheffé topic.
scenes.check: Three things to notice. The bias is positive and shrinks like 1/n, so consistency and bias at finite n sit together without contradiction — a question that offers 'it is consistent, therefore unbiased' is offering a false implication. The bias-corrected version is not a new discovery: it is the same (n−1)/ΣX that Lehmann–Scheffé produced, and the same estimator the Cramér–Rao topic showed does NOT attain the variance floor. And the whole calculation turned on E[1/Y] ≠ 1/E[Y]; if you got bias zero, that is the step to re-examine.

scenes.title: Six statements — verdict on each before you look
scenes.objective: Practise the per-statement discipline the real multi-statement items demand.
scenes.intro: Give every statement a true or false verdict first. In the exam these six would be one question scored all or nothing, so a verdict you skipped is a mark you gambled.

items.claim: Method of moments estimators are always unbiased.
items.why: False. They are consistent, not unbiased. σ̃² = (1/n)Σ(xᵢ−x̄)² has expectation (n−1)σ²/n, and λ̃ = n/ΣX for the exponential rate has bias λ/(n−1).

items.claim: For U(0,θ), the moment estimator 2x̄ can be smaller than the largest observation.
items.why: True, and that is its fatal defect — the estimate then lies in a region the likelihood assigns probability zero. The MLE x₍ₙ₎ cannot do this.

items.claim: The method of moments cannot be applied to the Cauchy distribution.
items.why: True. The Cauchy has no finite mean, so there is no first population moment to equate the sample mean to. The sample mean of a Cauchy sample does not converge.

items.claim: For the exponential distribution, the method of moments and maximum likelihood give different estimators of the rate.
items.why: False — they give the same estimator, n/ΣXᵢ. The two methods coincide for several standard one-parameter families, including the Poisson and the Bernoulli.

items.claim: Least squares estimation requires the errors to be normally distributed.
items.why: False. Gauss–Markov requires a correctly specified linear mean, full-rank design, zero-mean errors and uncorrelated homoscedastic errors. Normality is what makes least squares coincide with maximum likelihood, not what makes it BLUE.

items.claim: For multinomial data, the minimum chi-square and maximum likelihood estimators are asymptotically equivalent.
items.why: True under the regularity conditions for the multinomial model. The minimum chi-square, modified minimum chi-square and MLE then share the same limiting distribution, though they differ at finite n.

scenes.title: Transfer — least squares as a moment condition
scenes.objective: Derive the normal equations from two moment conditions, and see the three methods as one.
scenes.problem: Take the simple linear model yᵢ = β₀ + β₁xᵢ + εᵢ with E[εᵢ] = 0 and E[xᵢεᵢ] = 0. Treat these two conditions as moment conditions and derive the estimating equations for β₀ and β₁. Show they are the ordinary least squares normal equations, and solve them.
hints: Direction — a moment condition says a population expectation is zero. The method of moments replaces that expectation by its sample average and solves. So write each condition with εᵢ replaced by yᵢ − β₀ − β₁xᵢ, then average over the sample and set the average to zero.

Method — two conditions, two unknowns, so you will get two linear equations. Expand the sums and group the β terms on one side. Compare what you get with the normal equations as you learned them for regression.
Next step — to solve, use the first equation to express β₀ in terms of β₁, substitute into the second, and recognise the result as a ratio of sums of cross-products about the means.

solution.say: Replace each population condition by its sample analogue, with the residual in place of the error.
solution.math:
(1/n) Σ (yᵢ − β₀ − β₁xᵢ) = 0     (i)
(1/n) Σ xᵢ(yᵢ − β₀ − β₁xᵢ) = 0    (ii)

solution.say: Clear the 1/n and expand. These are the normal equations.
solution.math:
Σyᵢ = n β₀ + β₁ Σxᵢ          (i′)
Σxᵢyᵢ = β₀ Σxᵢ + β₁ Σxᵢ²      (ii′)

solution.say: Divide (i′) by n to get the intercept in terms of the slope.
solution.math: ȳ = β₀ + β₁x̄   ⇒   β̂₀ = ȳ − β̂₁x̄

solution.say: Substitute into (ii′) and collect the β₁ terms.
solution.math: Σxᵢyᵢ − n x̄ȳ = β₁ ( Σxᵢ² − n x̄² )

solution.say: Both sides are now sums of squares and cross-products about the means.
solution.math: S_xy = β₁ S_xx   ⇒   β̂₁ = S_xy / S_xx

solution.say: Note what the first condition alone has delivered.
solution.math: β̂₀ = ȳ − β̂₁x̄  ⇒  the fitted line passes through (x̄, ȳ), always

scenes.answer: The two moment conditions give Σ(yᵢ − β₀ − β₁xᵢ) = 0 and Σxᵢ(yᵢ − β₀ − β₁xᵢ) = 0 — precisely the OLS normal equations — with solution β̂₁ = S_xy/S_xx and β̂₀ = ȳ − β̂₁x̄. Least squares is the method of moments applied to the conditions 'the errors have zero mean' and 'the errors are uncorrelated with the regressor'.
scenes.check: Two things to take away. First, nothing in this derivation mentioned a distribution: the estimator came out of two expectations being zero, which is why least squares needs no normality. Second, the same estimator arrives from minimising a sum of squares, from maximising a normal likelihood, and from these moment conditions — the Berkeley note in the references adds a Bayesian route as a fourth. When a question asks you to 'derive the least squares estimators', any of these is a valid derivation, and the moment route is the shortest to write.

scenes.title: What you should now be able to do unaided
scenes.objective: Close the loop before the test.
body: Count the unknown parameters, write that many moment equations, and solve them — dividing one by the other when a parameter appears in both.
Quote the standard results from memory: Gamma β̃ = m₂/x̄ and α̃ = x̄²/m₂; U(a,b) endpoints x̄ ∓ √(3m₂); U(0,θ) gives 2x̄; N(μ,σ²) gives x̄ and m₂ with divisor n.
Claim consistency and asymptotic normality, and refuse to claim unbiasedness, efficiency or uniqueness.
Check every moment estimate against the parameter space, and against the sample maximum for a uniform.
Say immediately why the method fails for the Cauchy, and that the failure is the answer.
Write the minimum chi-square and modified minimum chi-square criteria, and name the data they need.
Derive the least squares normal equations by either route, and keep straight that normality is what joins least squares to maximum likelihood rather than something least squares assumes.
The mastery test is ten unseen questions across all of this. Hints are off. The pass is 80% overall with 70% floors on the numerical and multi-statement items.

scenes.title: Mastery test
scenes.objective: Demonstrate it independently, on unseen questions.
